newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma mulling $750 mln road bond plan.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma mulling $750 mln road bond plan.

text.p: A proposal expected to go before the Oklahoma State Legislature this session seeks permission for a $750 million lease-back road building program, a state senator said.

"Bond rates are extremely good right now," said State Senator Larry Dickerson, D-District Four, the bill's author. The bill seeks enabling legislation to take money out of Oklahoma growth revenue and pledge it for the state road building plan, he said.
The Oklahoma legislature convenes its annual session on February 3, Dickerson said.

Under the proposal, the Oklahoma Department of Transportation would develop the building plan, he said. The state's Turnpike's authority would then sell the bonds, build the roads and then lease them back to the DOT.

"Our state bond adviser has indicated that he believes these bonds would be triple-A rated, and because they would be handled through the turnpike authority, they would be double tax exempt," Dickerson said.
A senate press release said the turnpike authority would issue 20-year bonds over three years to finance the $750 million construction cost.
Given inflation concerns, issuing $750 million bonds that way makes more financial sense than selling smaller issues over a longer time frame, Dickerson said.
In addition, concern exists over declining gas and diesel taxes--the DOT's main revenue streams--which have been declining for the past several years, he said.
The senator said he has requested that the Oklahoma DOT repond to the legislative leadership on or before April 19, which about six weeks before the session ends.
Oklahoma's eight different transportation districts would benefit largely evenly from the proposed program, which Dickerson said is expected to generate broad-based support.
While two previous road building proposals failed to secure legislative approval, he said. One failed because it dealt only with metropolitan areas, Dickerson said.
"And the other plan that was put forth simply didn't put any new dollars into the Department of Transportation's existing budget, so as I said it was taking a pie and slicing it smaller," he said.
The senator, who's district includes LeFlore and Sequoyah counties, is chairman of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on General Government and Transportation.
